Placeholder operand address inside the second screen (print_string's store).
Row 12, column 12 of the second screen.
Third page of the second screen.
Fourth page of the second screen.
Twenty cells in the second screen's bottom row where the title keeps the two alternative texts of its top line ("GAME  OVER" and the other), copied from top_text.
Bottom row, column 36 of the second screen: the credits digit.
The eight sprite pointers of the second screen.
Sprite pointers 2-7 of the second screen.

Sprites $60-$67 ($5800-$59FF), 24 by 21 multicolour, 64 bytes each: the player's eight walking and standing frames, four facing each way (frames 0-7). Both players share them; only the colour differs. The first nine bytes of sprite $60 are cleared when a round is drawn.
Round that skip_rounds is heading for. Like the thirteen variables after it, it lives in the unused 64th byte of a sprite.
$FF once the objects have been ended for a bonus scene, so end_all_objects does nothing a second time.

Set to 2-5 by special item 7: how many times in a row the screen flashes and the giant block falls. Each time no block is on screen and the count is not zero the pass loop starts another, and the count goes down by one when a block ends.
Non-zero while the giant falling block is on screen.
Counts passes (draw_objects increments it); its low bits time the fire runs and the Barons' animation. Bonus scenes reuse it as the number of blocks left.

Next level whose leftover bubbles turn into food when it is cleared: when a round with this number starts, a food item is chosen for it ((level × 2 + 9), reduced below $2F) and this is moved on by food_round_step plus one. 0 at the start of a game, so round 1 is always one.
Step added to next_food_round each time it is reached, itself growing by one: 3 at the start, so the food rounds are 1, 5, 10, 16, 23 and so on.
Sprites $68-$6B: the player blowing a bubble, two frames facing each way (frames 8-$0B).
The state players are in while a timed power lasts: $10 normally, $18 during the freeze item; round_timers puts players in that state back to 1 when the round ends.
State given to an enemy that gets out of its bubble: $0A normally, $16 (frozen) during the freeze item.
Non-zero while the nine-sprite boss (or the ending's figure) is on screen: makes the bottom interrupt position it.

Sprites $6C-$72: the player's death. Sprites $6C-$6E with the last blowing frame are the four spinning frames ($0B-$0E); sprites $6F-$72 are four frames of the dragon with a ring turning over its head (frames $0F-$12), which loop until the death sequence ends.
Level after which the next secret door may appear: $12 at the start, then 10 more each time, jumping to $4E after the door of round 50.
One bit per player who has not yet lost a life (1, 2 or 3 at the start); while any is set, secret doors can appear.
Thunder shots the boss can still take; while it is beaten, the countdown of that state.
The last EXTEND letter a vent released (0-4), to which the next letter round adds its random step. Kept in the spare byte of a sprite.
Sprites $70-$72: three of the four looping frames of the dragon with a ring over its head.
Number of the tune last started with play_tune.
Sprites $73-$7E: enemy kind 2, the white wind-up robot. Twelve frames: four walking each way, three tumbling when thrown, and one small picture inside a bubble ring that is shown while it is held.
Sprites $7F-$8A: enemy kind 3, the grey spiky creature, in the same twelve-frame arrangement.
Sprites $8B-$96: enemy kind 4, the green hooded head on a coiled spring, twelve frames.
Sprites $97-$9E: enemy kind 5, the pale green flyer, eight frames: four flying, three tumbling, one in a bubble.
Sprites $9F-$AA: enemy kind 6, the purple whale-shaped flyer, twelve frames.
Sprites $AB-$B2: enemy kind 7, the green-cloaked one with a red face, eight frames: two walking each way, three tumbling, one in a bubble.
Sprites $B3-$BA: enemy kind 8, the white robed one, eight frames.
Sprites $BB-$C0: enemy kind 9, the white robot on cyan legs, six frames: two walking, three tumbling, one in a bubble. The last sprite ends at $703F.

Music data kept in the last sprite slots ($7040-$7304): five eight-byte drum and bass patterns that several tunes call, then the voices of tunes 2 (the boss round), 3 (the freeze), 4 (game over), 6 (EXTEND), 8 (hurry up), 9 (the Barons), 10 (the secret room) and 11 (the ending). Events are a note and a length index, or a command with bit 7 set (music_command_table).
Music command $80, start of a repeat: store the count that follows on the voice's stack, push the position after it, and go on.
Music command $82, end of a repeat: count down the voice's top repeat; if more remain go back to the pushed position, else drop it and go on.
Music command $84: copy 14 bytes from the address that follows into the voice's instrument block (frequency modulation only).
Music command $86: copy 29 bytes from the address that follows into the voice's instrument block at $F2AE, $F2CB or $F2E8.
Operand: low byte of the instrument block being filled.
Low bytes of the three voices' instrument blocks ($F2AE, $F2CB, $F2E8), patched into the copy loops.
Low bytes of the three voices' working copies of the modulation settings ($F31B, $F33E, $F361).
Music command $88: set the voice's transposition to the byte that follows.
Music command $8A: set the voice's arpeggio table to the byte that follows, an offset into the tables at $F2xx.
Music command $8C: route voices 1-3 through the filter ($D417 = $F7); the voice that drives the filter is left as it was.
Music command $8E: route this voice through the filter and let its instrument drive the cutoff.
Music command $90: filter routing $78, no voice through the filter, and the driving voice set to 3, which matches none of the three voices (0-2), so no note restarts the filter.
Music command $92: set the transposition from the first byte, then call the pattern at the address that follows.
Music command $94: push the position after the address that follows and continue at that address, a pattern call.
Operand: where the called pattern's address lies after the command byte, 1 or 2.
Music command $96: continue at the address that follows.
Music command $98: return from a pattern; at the bottom of the voice's stack the voice is finished instead and is switched off.
Load the music pointer from the top of the voice's stack.
Music command $9A: copy 16 bytes from the address that follows into the filter sweep block at $F30B.
Music command $9C: set the instrument's sustain and release byte to $FF and its release time to $FE in the voice's instrument block, so notes ring on; the gate time is not changed.
Push the music pointer on the voice's stack.
Replace the music pointer with the address stored at it + Y.
Add A to the music pointer.
Filter routing value for each voice: $F1, $F2, $F4.
Offset of each voice's instrument block from $F2AE: 0, $1D, $3A.
Offset of each voice's working block from $F31B: 0, $23, $46.
Each voice's first stack index: 0, $0C, $18.
Offset of each voice's registers in the SID: 0, 7, 14, and one past the last register of each (7, 14, 21).
Each voice's register offset plus seven, the top of the loop that writes a voice's seven registers.

Sprites $D1-$D8 ($7440-$763F): the large bubble the players float in at the start of a game and between rounds, four sprites to a bubble (two rows of two) in two animation steps. The dragon inside is drawn across the middle, its upper part at the bottom of the top pair and its lower part at the top of the bottom pair.
Sprites $D9-$E1 ($7640-$787F): the round-100 boss facing right, three rows of three sprites. Sprites 2-7 show the top two rows and irq_boss_lower moves three of them down for the third.
Sprites $E2-$EA ($7880-$7ABF): the boss in its beaten state (frame 9), nine sprites.
Reverse the order of the four bit pairs of A: a multicolour byte mirrored left to right.

Round 100 only: make the nine mirrored boss sprites at $7C40-$7E7F (shown while the boss moves right) from the nine at $7640-$787F (shown while it moves left) by mirroring each of their 21 rows of three bytes; the three sprites of each row of the figure also change places.
Low bytes of the nine source sprites of build_boss_mirror.
High bytes of the nine source sprites.
Low bytes of the nine mirrored sprites' addresses.
High bytes of the nine mirrored sprites' addresses.
Print the right-hand panel (1UP, 2UP, TOP, CREDITS), the scores and lives, GAME OVER for a player who is out, and the number of credits plus one.
The string "CREDITS" for row $17, column $21 in colour 3, a second position, and the two digit cells that draw_panel fills in.
The credits digit of that string, written before it is printed, and the terminator.
Mark the five fire runs free and switch the water stream off.
Entry of both raster handlers: save A, X and Y in zero page, clear decimal mode, save the processor port and select RAM with I/O ($35).
Wait five frames.
Wait ten frames.
Wait A frames, counting in $0100.
Draw handler for type $16, a bubble on its first pass: make it type 0 and draw it as the smallest stage.
Draw handler for type $36: free the object slot.
Print "GAME OVER" on the panel in the rows of player X.
Return in $40/$41 the address in the collision map of object X's cell, and in A its sub-row.
Object type $28, the fireball of enemy kind 3: toggles its animation phase and flies as a horizontal shot that vanishes (type $38) at a wall and kills a player it touches.
Add 10 points to player X.
Add packed-decimal A to the score byte at $0400 + Y and carry into the bytes above it: Y selects the player and the digit pair.
Special item $21, the door of round 50: skip to round 70 (level $45).
Special item $22, round 100's potion: count the player's weapon charge down, which sets bit 7 and arms the thunder bubbles.
576 bytes, zero in the loaded game: the nine mirrored boss sprites built on round 100 (sprites $F1-$F9); the second half is shared with the item sprite buffers.
Three 128-byte buffers (sprites $F4-$F9), zero in the loaded game: food sprites built from glyphs, the giant food, and the bonus pictures.
In the item sprite buffer: eight bytes patched into the giant picture of kind 1.
In the item sprite buffer: a byte of pixels that effect_six_sprites_b writes into its picture.
In the item sprite buffer: eight more patched bytes for giant kind 1.
Second 128-byte item sprite buffer (sprites $F6-$F7).
In the second buffer: a byte of pixels that effect_six_sprites_b writes into its picture.
In the second buffer: another byte of pixels of that picture.
Third 128-byte item sprite buffer (sprites $F8-$F9).
In the third buffer: the last byte of pixels that effect_six_sprites_b writes into its picture.
Read the keyboard: RUN/STOP pauses. The actors stop, the timers are saved, and the game waits for the key to be released, pressed again and released.
Wait a frame, then read the keyboard.
Select keyboard row 7 and return the column bits (through the cracker's stub) with the zero flag set when the value is $7F: RUN/STOP and no other key of the row.
Q (column 6 of row 7) quits: stop everything, silence the SID, drop the return address and go back to the title after 25 frames.
The message of the secret room: rows of character codes $85-$97 from the room's own alphabet with position codes, printed by print_string.
Give player X the ordinary bubble: travel $88, reload 8, range flag 4, speed 4, no fire breath, no bonuses, not fast, no weapon. On round 100 falls into the boss set-up.

Round 100: the special item is the potion ($22) and the points item number $51, both due at once; reload time 8 for both players; eight "enemies" so the round cannot be cleared; and the blow routine marks every bubble with its owner.
Special item $14, an umbrella: skip to three rounds ahead.

Per round: bits 4-7 complete the special item's row; bit 0 says whether the round's vents release special bubbles at all, and bits 1-3 which kinds (water, fire, thunder); when bit 0 is set the round may instead be a letter round, chosen at random.

The air currents of all 100 rounds, a record per round. The first byte is the record's length, or zero for none; a first byte with bit 7 set is a one-byte record meaning "use round n's currents" (rounds 2, 36 and 48 use round 1's, round 52 round 50's). Entries follow from the second byte. A rectangle is three bytes: byte 0 has bit 7 set, the direction in bits 5-6 (0 up, 1 right, 2 down, 3 left) and the column in bits 0-4; byte 1 has the row in bits 3-7 and the top three bits of the width; byte 2 the last two bits of the width in bits 6-7 and the height in bits 0-4, width and height both stored less one. A single byte without bit 7 in an entry's place mirrors the left half of the map onto the right, swapping left and right currents.

Per round: bit 0 opens the top row at columns 9-12 and bit 1 at columns 19-22; bits 2 and 3 do the same for the bottom row. Bits 4-5 are the air current of the top row and bits 6-7 of the bottom row. Players, enemies and bubbles pass through an opening from one edge of the screen to the other.

The layouts of the 100 rounds, a bit per cell: 23 rows (the top and bottom rows come from level_gaps) of 32 columns. A full layout is 92 bytes, four per row; a round whose level_pattern byte has bit 7 set stores only the left half, 46 bytes, and is mirrored. 55 rounds are halves and 45 full, 6,670 bytes that end exactly at $DFFF: the last 4 KB lie in the RAM under the video and sound chips, which is why unpack_layout switches the I/O out.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 16 (a mirrored half, 46 bytes) starts here.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 31 (full, 92 bytes) starts here.
The layouts continue here, in the RAM under the I/O area ($D000-$DFFF), read only with $01 = $30.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 43 (full, 92 bytes) starts here.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 57 (a mirrored half, 46 bytes) starts here.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 71 (a mirrored half, 46 bytes) starts here.
Layout data: byte 22 of round 72's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the first cell), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 23 of round 72's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the second cell), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 13 of round 73's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the score table's upper rule), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 13 of round 74's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the title's top line), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 48 of round 75's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the second page), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 20 of round 78's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the round banner's first row), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 75 of round 78's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (a placeholder operand of print_string), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 8 of round 79's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the round banner's second row), which is what every reference to it in the code means.
Layout data: byte 28 of round 79's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the third page), which is what every reference to it in the code means.

Layout data: byte 73 of round 80's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the score table's lower rule), which is what every reference to it in the code means.
Layout data: byte 8 of round 84's layout. The label is here because the same address, with the I/O switched in, is colour RAM (the fourth page), which is what every reference to it in the code means.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 85 (full, 92 bytes) starts here.
Layouts continue: the layout of round 97 (full, 92 bytes) starts here.

Build round `level` in the buffer at $5400: reset the buffer roles, copy the round's 8-byte wall tile to character $15 and its 2 by 2 wall block (from wall_blocks by the round's pattern number, or four copies of the tile when the number is $64 or more) to characters $16-$19, take the two multicolours from level_colours, set the timers, unpack the layout bitmap and draw it.

Draw the unpacked layout at $8B00 (25 rows of four bytes, a bit per cell of 32 columns) into the screen at $5400: a set bit is the wall tile (character $15), and each tile casts a shadow on the empty cells to its right, below and diagonally (characters $0A-$0F). Then the 2 by 2 wall blocks down both sides in columns 0-1 and 30-31, and a little tidying of the top row.

Fill the collision map at $8500 with the round's air currents. Starts by giving every cell of a row the direction stored in the low two bits of the row's fourth layout byte, then reads the round's record in air_current_data: a record that is a single byte with bit 7 set means "the same as round n"; otherwise it is a list of rectangles, each three bytes giving direction, column, row, width and height, written over the map; a zero byte instead of a rectangle mirrors the left half of every row onto the right with left and right swapped.
Still build_air_currents: decoding one rectangle. The label is here only because a store in hurry_up carries $E200 as its as-loaded operand; its high byte is patched before it runs.
Add 40 to the pointer in $04/$05 and decrement X.

Unpack round X's layout into $8B00 with the I/O switched out ($01 = $30), because the layouts lie in $C5F2-$DFFF, partly under the chips. Each earlier round takes 46 bytes if bit 7 of its byte in level_pattern is set and 92 if not. The round's byte in level_gaps gives the openings of the top and bottom rows and their air currents. A full layout is 23 rows of four bytes copied as they are; a half layout holds two bytes a row, and the other two are their mirror image. After each row the top two bits of that row's first byte are forced on: the left wall.
The same for the layout at $40/$41 with X the round: used directly for the secret room.
Operand of the patched JSR that unpacks a layout row.
High byte of the patched row unpacker call.
Copy two layout bytes to the row (called twice a row for a full layout).
Copy one layout byte to $8B04,X and advance.
Write the mirror images of the row's first two bytes into its third and fourth, in reverse order.
Return the byte at $8B02,X with its eight bits in reverse order, and advance X.

Write the four bytes of a top or bottom row as two halves, from two bits of the gap code: the left half is $FF $FF, or $FF $87 with an opening at columns 9-12; the right half is $FF $FF, or $E1 $FF with an opening at columns 19-22.
One half of unpack_gap_row: take the next bit of the gap code; clear selects index 0 (no opening), set keeps the index the caller loaded (1 for the left half, 2 for the right).
Low bytes of the two row unpackers (full, mirrored), patched into the JSR at $E30B.
High bytes of the two row unpackers.
First byte of a half row by index: $FF (no opening), $FF (left half with its opening), $E1 (right half with its opening).
Second byte of a half row by index: $FF (no opening), $87 (left half with its opening), $FF (right half with its opening).
Black border and background, sprites off, colour RAM to 0, and both screen buffers filled with spaces.
Fill the screen at $5400 with spaces.
Print both scores and the top score on the panel of the screen on display, after replacing the top score with any player's score that has passed it.
Print the three packed-decimal bytes at $0400 + X as six digits at the address in $40/$41, blanking leading zeros.
Compare the score at $0400 + A with the top score; if it is higher, copy it there and record that player's round as the top round.
Twelve bytes of code nothing reaches: an earlier form of the leading-zero test that print_score_digit now does.

Print the string at X (low) and Y (high) on both screen buffers and colour RAM. A byte below $10 sets the colour, $10 ends the string, $1F is followed by a column and a row and moves the print position (which is patched into the three store instructions at $E472), and any other byte is a character code plus $20.
Operand: the column from a position code, added to the row's address.
The three stores of print_string, to the screen at $5000, the screen at $5400 and colour RAM; their operands are the print position and are advanced after each character.
Operand: print position in the screen at $5000.
High byte of the print position in the screen at $5000.
Operand: print position in the screen at $5400.
High byte of the print position in the screen at $5400.
Operand: print position in colour RAM.
High byte of the print position in colour RAM.
Wait until the frame counter changes: the next bottom raster interrupt.
Copy the screen at $5000 to the clean copy at $8B00 and to the second buffer at $5400.
Copy the round-number glyphs to the second character set and put their two characters at the top left of the second buffer.
Arm intro_step to animate the bubble sprites (turns the RTS at $E539 into the LDA of the code behind it) and run it once.

One frame of the players floating in their bubbles: each live player's four bubble sprites (two rows of two) are placed round the player's position, sprite X high bits set as needed, and all eight are coloured; when armed, the code after $E539 also sets the eight sprites' shapes (the cycling between the two sets is done by irq_top).
RTS patched to LDA #$D4: the code that follows then sets the bubble sprites' shapes, $D1-$D4 for sprites 0-3 and $D5-$D8 for sprites 4-7.
Operand of the instruction made at $E539 when intro_step is armed: $D4, the first shape of a floating bubble.

The armed tail of intro_step: for X = 3 down to 0 give sprite X the shape in A and sprite X + 4 that shape plus four, in both screens' pointer tables, and step A back by one (the SBC #$04 runs with carry clear and undoes the ADC #$04 and one more).
Sprite X high-bit masks for the two players' right-hand bubble sprites.

Bring the players into the round in their bubbles: disarm the shape code, clear the path buffers at $8B00-$8EFF, and for each player work out a straight line from where they are to their starting place (X $2C or $EC, Y $DD) with trace_line; then replay both paths a point a frame, moving the bubbles, and finally clear split_line.
High bytes of the two players' path buffers ($8B00 and $8D00; Y coordinates go in the page after each).
X of the starting place of each player: $2C and $EC.

Record the points of a straight line from ($23,$24) to (X,Y) in the path buffer whose page is A: Bresenham's algorithm stepping along the longer axis, one point for each step, X coordinates in one page and Y in the next.

Make the glyphs of the five letter bubbles as 2 by 2 blocks for the panel and the EXTEND scene: copy the background (characters $11-$14, the wall-block copy, 32 bytes from $4088) to $0108, then for each of the letters E, X, T, N and D build 32 bytes at $4250 onward as the background masked by the bubble mask, ORed with that letter bubble's picture, and ANDed with extend_mask; finally copy characters $40-$5F to the second character set.
Draw each player's collected letters down the side of the playfield (columns 0-1 for player 1, 30-31 for player 2, from row 10), a 2 by 2 block per letter, in both screen buffers and the clean copy.
One player's column of letters: address in A (high) and Y (low), X the player.
First character of each letter's 2 by 2 block on the panel, for D, N, E, T, X, E in the order the bits are tested.
Fill all 1,024 cells of colour RAM with A.
Draw handler for type $2A, the boulder: picture $38 + sub-column.
Draw handler for type $24, the falling flame: picture $34 + sub-column, shifted down by its sub-row.
Per Baron: 0 or 2, which way it faces, set by baron_move from where its player is.
Draw handler for types $2E and $30, the Barons: picture $30-$33 by facing and a two-step animation that changes every second pass.
Draw handler for types 0-$14, every plain, special and letter bubble: picture type × 2 + sub-column, shifted down by the sub-row. Falls into the renderer.

With A the picture number: patch the renderer's six table operands, three for the picture's 16-byte graphic columns (bubble_gfx_lo/hi) and three for its masks (bubble_mask_lo/hi), each column 16 bytes after the last.

The bubble renderer. An object covers three cells across and two or three rows of cells. Starting in the lowest row of cells and working upward line by line, it finds the glyphs now on screen there, replaces the three cells with fresh dynamic characters (numbered from next_glyph), and writes each new glyph as the old glyph ANDed with the picture's mask and ORed with its graphic, for the 16 lines of the picture; the lines of the cells below and above the picture are copied unchanged. The object's sub-row (rows_left) decides how many lines are copied before the picture's bottom line.
Operand: address of the mask column for the first cell of a row.
High byte of the first mask column's address.
Operand: address of the graphic column for the first cell.
High byte of the first graphic column's address.
Operand: mask column for the second cell.
High byte of the second mask column's address.
Operand: graphic column for the second cell.
High byte of the second graphic column's address.
Operand: mask column for the third cell.
High byte of the third mask column's address.
Operand: graphic column for the third cell.
High byte of the third graphic column's address; from here the renderer's row loop continues.
Move the renderer up to the row of cells above: find the three glyphs on screen there, hand out three more dynamic characters and continue the merge. A picture is merged from its bottom line upward.

Once a pass: note the chain and letter counts, start the dynamic glyphs again at character $5E of the back character set, and for every object in use remember where it was drawn the last two passes, compute its screen address and jump to its draw handler through object_draw_table. Afterwards pay each player's chain bonus if the chain did not grow this pass, and redraw the EXTEND letters if they changed.
Operand of draw_objects' JMP: the low byte selects the entry of object_draw_table.
Common return of the draw handlers that draw nothing: skip the nine glyphs this object would have used.
Common return after drawing: advance the glyph pointer by 72 bytes and go on to the next object.

For actor X: split its position into a map cell and the offsets within it (sub_x, sub_y) and set map_ptr to the collision-map cell one column left of the actor's left cell and three rows above the row its Y gives ((Y - $15) / 8), which is the upper of the two rows a standing actor's body covers. Fixed offsets from it then reach the cells the body covers ($01, $02, $29, $2A), those beside it ($00, $28 and $03, $2B), the floor under it ($51, $52) and the row below that ($79, $7A).
Random number in A: shifts and mixes the two state bytes and exclusive-ORs the low byte of CIA 1's timer B.

Enemy kinds 3, 7 and 8 (states 3, 7, 8), the three that shoot along their row: decide whether to shoot, then behave as the walker. While a shot is being readied it counts down; then it fires: a fireball for kind 3 (type $28), a boulder for kind 8 ($2A), or for kind 7 a bottle ($2C) that comes back and that it waits for.

Enemy kind 2 (state 2) and the movement of the shooters. Falls when nothing is underfoot. On the ground it follows its input bits: bit 0 walks left, bit 1 right, bit 2 starts a jump. chase_timer decides whether it may climb: when allowed it jumps to a platform it finds overhead or across a gap at the end of its floor.
Every second call advance the actor's frame, wrapping within its facing's set of frames (frame count and mask from the per-kind tables).
Fall with the tail patched so that the two-frame animation runs afterwards.
An enemy with nothing underfoot: fall two pixels a call, wrapping at the bottom, until a floor is under it; then clear the falling flag.
JMP or BIT, patched by the three entries of the fall routine to choose what runs when the enemy lands.

The code the patched fall_tail_a falls into for the bolt dropper, kind 9 (enemy_fall_then_flip turns the JMP into a BIT): once landed, set the enemy's heading bit towards its target player (left unless the player's X is greater than its own) and go on to the two-frame animation.
JMP whose target the three entries of the fall routine patch: the walk animation, the two-frame animation or a plain return.
Operand of fall_tail_b.
High byte of fall_tail_b's target.
The plain return used as the fall's tail by enemy_fall_plain.
Fall with no animation afterwards.
Start an enemy's jump: 31 steps, straight up, with the jump-request bit (bit 2) of its control byte cleared.

An enemy rising or landing from a jump. A jump straight up (counter $1F) starts with 16 calls of waiting, in which the enemy looks the other way and back on every fourth call. Then 15 steps up: by jump_arc_enemy when it has no side flag, or one pixel a step when it has. Then down, by jump_arc_enemy or with a side flag by jump_arc_drift, until a floor is crossed. With a side flag set it drifts two pixels a step and stops drifting at a wall.
Walk left two pixels, turning the enemy to face left first; at a wall reverse its direction bits.
Move the actor sideways by A unless the map cell at offset Y from map_ptr is solid, in which case reverse its direction bits.
Step four pixels left.
Step four pixels right.
Walk right two pixels, turning the enemy to face right first.

The shooter's count has run out: put its readied shot (the object slot it reserved) on the row it stands on, directly in front of it (two columns from its own column on the side it faces), as the shot of its kind, or cancel it if a wall is in the way.

An enemy standing on a floor with no shot out, one call in four at random: if it faces its target player and that player is level with it (or, one time in 32, higher up; never when the player is lower), reserve a free object slot as a readied shot (type $42) and start the count of seven calls; it will not try again for $96 calls.
The two-frame animation again, used only by kind 9, the bolt dropper: its idle animation, its walk and the tail of its fall. The hopper uses animate_two_frames.

Decide how an enemy pursues its target player. Level with the player: set the level flag, clear the climb flag and the jump bit. Higher than the player: clear both flags and the jump bit, so it does not climb. Lower than the player: each time its chase timer runs out (the period is the kind's value plus a random 0-31, set by start_round, not taken from the enemy record) set one of the two flags and clear the other, alternately, so it swaps between trying to climb and not. The decision is kept in the enemy's two chase flags.
Enemy kind 6 (state 6): flies diagonally two pixels a call, bouncing off walls, floors and ceilings.
Flying left: face left first, then move.
Move the flyer two pixels left unless a wall is in the way, in which case reverse its horizontal direction. On entry Y holds the opcode to store at fly_step.

Opcode patched by fly_left and fly_right with the byte their caller passes in Y: $60 (RTS) for the slow flyer, which ends the reversal there, or $BD for the fast one, which makes it an LDA $8520,X that runs on into fly_flip_facing. It is not a speed.
Operand bytes of the LDA that fly_step becomes for the fast flyer ($8520, the frame array).
When the fast flyer patches fly_step to an LDA: flip the actor's facing frames (EOR 4) as it bounces, then return.
Flying right: face right first, then move.
Move the flyer two pixels right unless a wall is in the way, in which case reverse. On entry Y holds the opcode to store at fly_step.

Move the flyer up by its speed; at the top of the screen (Y $15) wrap to the bottom if the bottom map row's cell in its column is open, and reverse its vertical direction if it is not; also reverse at a ceiling.
Move the flyer down by its speed; wrap from the bottom to the top through an opening; reverse at a floor.
Enemy kind 5 (state 5): flies diagonally, one pixel a call vertically and two horizontally, bouncing the same way, with a four-frame animation.
Every second call step the actor's frame through 0-3.
The score table: stars, the table's text, each player's last score and round, the two player sprites, then reset the first-round flags and go to the title's key loop.

As loaded: LDA #$FF / STA level / JMP title_patch, which sets the round before the first. title_patch replaces these seven bytes with STX level / LDA #3 / STA $D015 on the first visit. The cracker's menu stores its starting round minus two in the operand at $F044, so its choice applies to the first game only.

Print the three scores, fill in each player's round and the top round, and wait for the 1 or 2 key (row 7, columns 0 and 3), each frame drawing a random number; 2 adds the second player. Then count the round up from $FF to 0 and play a game.

The LDA # in title_loop whose operand at $F073 play_game sets to 1 (the store at $0910): the colour given to the ten cells of the title's top line, 0 (black, so the line does not show) as loaded and 1 (white) once a game has been started.

Operand of the LDA # at $F072 (see title_two_up). From here the rest of the title loop: prints each player's last round and the top round (two digits; 100 for round 100; the three characters ALL for a finished game) and waits for the key.
The wait itself: read the keyboard through read_keys_wait.
The score table's string: BUBBLE BOBBLE, COMMODORE CONVERSION BY SOFTWARE CREATIONS, SCORE, ROUND, TOP, WRITTEN BY STEPHEN RUDDY, CREDITS 10 and PRESS 1 OR 2 TO PLAY.
Thirteen offsets into the secret room's layout rows where single bytes are patched.
The thirteen bytes patched at those offsets, shaping the secret room.

For each player compare the score with the next entry of extra_life_scores; on reaching it add a life, move to the next step and request sound 3. Also, when a tune is not playing over it, start the pending sound effect: number 0-5 from sound_request or the jump request.
Low bytes of the six sound effect records.
High bytes of the six sound effect records.

Called from init_round_state. On round 73 it writes air current 2 (down) into the four cells of the bottom row's left opening (columns 9-12), in the map row and its three copies below. Then it sets the threshold at $0DC7 that decides how overlapping bubbles part. The code loads $1E into Y, or $E6 on rounds 35 and 97, but the store is an STA, so what is written is A: the level number (2 on round 73). The value in Y is never used.
Addresses of the fifteen music commands $80, $82 ... $9C, entered through the JMP at $F57B whose operand's low byte is the command with its top two bits flipped.
Ten short arpeggio tables, lists of semitone offsets that a voice steps through one per frame (0, 7 and 12 are the fifth and the octave), selected by music command $8A.
Low bytes of the three voices' return stacks, four entries each at $F28A, $F296 and $F2A2 by voice_stack_base.
High bytes of the voices' return stacks.
Repeat counts kept on the voices' stacks by the loop commands.

Voice 1's instrument block, 29 bytes filled by music command $86: eleven bytes of frequency modulation (four steps of rate and duration, a delay, flags), the pulse sweep, pulse width, waveform, attack/decay, sustain/release, gate time and release time. Voices 2 and 3 have theirs at $F2CB and $F2E8.
Arpeggio table address, low byte, in the voice's instrument block (set by music command $8A).
Arpeggio table address, high byte, always $F2.
Frequency modulation flags of the instrument: bit 3 selects an arpeggio, bit 0 and bit 7 choose whether the modulation repeats.
Pulse sweep flags of the instrument, cleared when a tune starts.
The instrument's starting pulse width, low byte.
The instrument's starting pulse width, high byte.
The instrument's SID control byte: waveform and gate.
The instrument's attack and decay.
The instrument's sustain and release.
Frames the gate stays on, counted from the end of the note.
Frames the voice keeps sounding after the gate goes off; then the next two voices' blocks.
Per voice: non-zero while notes may sound on it; start_sfx clears voice 1's so the tune leaves it to the effect.
Voice 2's enable flag.
Voice 3's enable flag.
Per voice: non-zero while the voice still has music to play; cleared when its stream ends.
Voice 2's data flag.
Voice 3's data flag.
Sixteen bytes of filter settings, loaded by music command $9A. The driver uses only the cutoff's two bytes ($F392, $F393).

Voice 1's working block, 35 bytes ($F31B-$F33D): the copy of its instrument's 24 modulation bytes and the counters that run them down. Voices 2 and 3 have theirs at $F33E and $F361. Its first word is the first frequency step's rate.
Working block: first frequency step, high byte of the rate.
Working block: second frequency step, rate low byte.
Working block: second frequency step, rate high byte.
Working block: third frequency step, rate low byte; for an arpeggio the frame counter between steps.
Working block: third frequency step, rate high byte.
Working block: fourth frequency step, rate low byte; for an arpeggio its speed in frames.
Working block: fourth frequency step, rate high byte.
Working block: duration of the first frequency step; for an arpeggio the low byte of its table.
Working block: duration of the second step; for an arpeggio the high byte of its table.
Working block: duration of the third step; for an arpeggio the base note.
Working block: duration of the fourth step; for an arpeggio the table's length.
Working block: frames before the modulation starts; for an arpeggio the current position.
Working block: the frequency modulation flags.
Working block: frames the pulse width sweeps one way.
Working block: frames it sweeps back.
Working block: frames before the pulse sweep starts.
Working block: the pulse sweep flags (0 for none).
Working block: amount added to the pulse width each frame on the way up, low byte.
Working block: high byte of that amount.
Working block: amount added on the way back, low byte.
Working block: high byte of the amount added to the pulse width on the way back.
Working block: the pulse width the sweep restarts from, low byte.
Working block: the pulse width the sweep restarts from, high byte.
Working block: the note's own frequency, low byte, which a repeating modulation returns to.
Working block: the note's own frequency, high byte.
Working block: the voice's control byte as last written.
Working block: the gate countdown.
Working block: the release countdown; 0 means the voice is silent.
Working block: frames left of the first frequency step.
Working block: frames left of the second frequency step.
Working block: frames left of the third frequency step.
Working block: frames left of the fourth frequency step.
Working block: frames left of the pulse sweep's upward half.
Working block: frames left of its downward half; voice 2's working block follows.
Voice 2's release countdown, zeroed by silence.
Voice 3's release countdown, zeroed by silence.
Working copy of the filter sweep, sixteen bytes.
Filter sweep settings: duration of its first half.
Filter sweep settings: duration of its second half.
Filter sweep settings: frames before it starts.
Filter sweep settings: a flag byte copied with the block but not read by the sweep; the byte after it is not read by anything found.
Written when a tune is silenced and when the voice that drives the filter goes quiet; nothing reads it.
The cutoff's starting value, low part.
The cutoff's starting value, high part.
Working copy of the cutoff's low part, written by filter_restart; nothing reads it.
Working copy of the cutoff's high part, written by filter_restart; nothing reads it.
Working copy of the first length byte of the filter settings, written by filter_restart; nothing reads or counts it down.
Working copy of the second length byte of the filter settings; nothing reads it.
Working copy of the delay byte of the filter settings; nothing reads it.
One byte before the note length table: lengths are indexed from 1. Also the sweep's flag byte.
Thirty-two note lengths in frames, multiples 1-32 of the tune's tempo, rebuilt by start_tune.
Low bytes of the SID frequency of each of the 95 notes, in semitones from the lowest.
High bytes of the 95 note frequencies.

Start the tune whose seven-byte record has its third voice's address at tune_table + Y and its tempo byte at tune_table + Y + 2: load the three voices' data addresses, reset each voice's transposition, stack and counters, and build the table of note lengths as multiples of the record's tempo byte.
Operand of start_tune's ADC: the tune's tempo, the number of frames in the shortest note length.
Reset the SID: write 8 then 0 to all 23 registers below the volume, stop the three voices and their effects, release the filter, and set full volume with the low-pass filter on ($1F).

Called when the voice that drives the filter starts a note: copy the sixteen filter settings to their working block, copy four of them on to further working bytes, and write the starting cutoff to the SID ($D415, $D416). Nothing changes the cutoff afterwards: the working bytes are never read, so no sweep runs.
Once a frame, for each voice: step its music if it still has data, and run its envelope and modulations while a note sounds. tune_playing counts the voices with data.
Count the voice's wait down; when it reaches zero read the next events.
Skip one byte and read the next event.
Skip A bytes and read the next event.
Read the voice's next event: a byte with bit 7 set is a command and goes through music_command_table; anything else is a note.
The JMP through music_command_table.
Operand of mus_dispatch: low byte of the table entry.

A note: values up to $5E are pitches (transposed, then looked up in freq_lo/freq_hi), $5F and above rests. Restarts the voice's oscillator with the test bit, loads frequency, pulse width, waveform and envelope from the instrument, restarts the pulse and frequency modulations and the filter if this voice drives it, and sets the gate time. The byte after the note indexes the table of lengths.
Operand: low byte of the voice's instrument block; from here voice_note copies the modulation settings into the working block.
Operand: low byte of the voice's working block.
Read the length byte, set the wait and remember where the voice continues.
Set the voice's working frequency back to the note's own, then reload the frequency modulation's four step counters from the instrument.
The reload alone, for a modulation that repeats.
Reload the pulse-width sweep from its starting value.
Reload the pulse sweep's two counters.

One frame of a sounding voice: count the gate time and then clear the gate bit; count the release and then silence the voice; sweep the pulse width up and down by the instrument's two rates; and either step an arpeggio through its table of semitone offsets or run the four-stage frequency modulation (vibrato and slides).

Start the sound effect whose 30-byte record is at A (low), Y (high) on voice 1: silence the voice, load pulse, control and envelope, the starting note, gate and release times, and the 24 modulation bytes, then restart the modulations.

Twelve tune records of seven bytes: the addresses of the three voices' data and a tempo, the number of frames in the shortest note.
